newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rule change for Bosnia polls, but problems remain.
newsitem.headline: Rule change for Bosnia polls, but problems remain.

text.p: The international community announced measures on Thursday to combat voting irregularities in Bosnia's local elections next month, but political wrangling cast doubt on whether the polls would be held on schedule.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the body supervising Bosnia's postwar elections, said the rules for the municipal elections had been changed to remove problems associated with votes cast by refugees abroad.

A meeting in Sarajevo of the Provisional Election Commission, the OSCE's top rule-making body for the elections, decided that refugees would now be allowed to vote only where they had been living in 1991.
Those who could prove residence in a different municipality since the Bosnian peace settlement was agreed last December would be allowed to vote there.
Municipal elections were due to have been held last September 14, along with general elections.
But the local elections were postponed until November 23 and 24, largely because it was found that Serb refugees were being put under pressure to vote in towns which had once had Moslem majorities.

Hrair Balian of the International Crisis Group, a private body monitoring the peace process, said the Serbs had manipulated the system before and would not like the new rule. "The Serbs will not accept this," he told Reuters.
OSCE spokesman David Foley said the election commission's ruling was "a crucial decision."

The OSCE has been in intense negotiations with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic to reverse her objections to the local polls being held under OSCE supervision and her assertion that the security situation was not favourable for elections.
"With regard to the negotiations with Mrs Plavsic, we have yet to reach closure on the issue," Foley said.

He said any decision by the election commission on whether the polls should be held would depend on a favourable outcome to consultations between representatives of the international community and the Bosnian factions, and this remained elusive.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, who has made repeated trips to Bosnia, was expected to visit Sarajevo next week to try to resolve the election issue.
Apart from the Bosnian factions, there is growing opposition within the international community to the polls being held next month.
Elizabeth Rehn, the United Nations human rights investigator for former Yugoslavia, said on Monday they should be postponed if human rights conditions could not be met.
